questions.stem: A new patient has mild asthma with symptoms twice a month. What is the preferred treatment?
questions.explanation: C is correct: for mild asthma, the preferred track is as-needed budesonide-formoterol, which puts a steroid into every rescue puff. A gives no inhaled steroid and raises the risk of severe attacks. B uses a long-acting bronchodilator alone, which is never done in asthma. D is the two-bronchodilator start for COPD.

questions.stem: Why is albuterol alone, with no inhaled steroid, no longer recommended for asthma?

options.text: It raises the risk of severe attacks

questions.explanation: A is correct: treating asthma with albuterol alone raises the risk of severe attacks, because asthma is inflammation that needs an inhaled steroid. B, thrush, is a side effect of inhaled steroids. C, cost, is not the reason. D is wrong because albuterol is a rescue inhaler in both asthma and COPD.

questions.stem: A patient has moderate asthma on the preferred track. Which regimen fits?

options.text: Budesonide-formoterol every day, plus extra puffs as needed

questions.explanation: A is correct: for moderate asthma, use budesonide-formoterol every day plus extra puffs when needed, called maintenance and reliever therapy. B has no inhaled steroid. C is a long-acting bronchodilator alone, never used in asthma. D is not a step on the preferred track for moderate asthma.

questions.stem: A patient with asthma brings a new prescription for salmeterol alone, with no inhaled steroid. What is the best action?

options.text: Tell the patient to stop their rescue inhaler
Contact the prescriber: asthma needs an inhaled steroid with any long-acting bronchodilator

questions.explanation: C is correct: never use a long-acting bronchodilator alone in asthma, without a steroid. A dispenses an unsafe regimen. B removes rescue therapy. D adds a rescue inhaler but still leaves out the inhaled steroid.

questions.stem: A patient with COPD had one hospital stay for a flare last year. Blood eosinophils are 120 cells/µL. What is the best starting therapy?
questions.explanation: B is correct: start two long-acting bronchodilators, and eosinophils are low, so no inhaled steroid yet. A is a steroid plus beta agonist combination, which is not encouraged as a start in COPD. C is not enough for a patient with a past flare. D is not one of the long-acting bronchodilators that come first in COPD.

questions.stem: A patient with COPD on tiotropium plus olodaterol keeps having flares. Blood eosinophils are 350 cells/µL. What is the best next step?

options.text: Stop the bronchodilators and use albuterol only

questions.explanation: A is correct: add an inhaled steroid when eosinophils are 300 or more or flares keep happening; this patient has both. B removes the long-acting bronchodilators that come first in COPD. C drops to a single bronchodilator. D ignores repeated flares.

questions.stem: Which statements correctly compare asthma and COPD treatment? Select all that apply.

options.text: In COPD, starting with only a steroid plus a long-acting beta agonist is encouraged
In asthma, the inhaled steroid comes first
In COPD, two long-acting bronchodilators come first
In asthma, never use a long-acting beta agonist alone

questions.explanation: B, C, and D are correct: asthma is inflammation, so the inhaled steroid comes first and a long-acting beta agonist is never used alone; in COPD, two long-acting bronchodilators come first. A is wrong because a steroid plus long-acting beta agonist start is not encouraged in COPD; if a steroid is needed, use triple therapy. E is wrong because COPD airflow does not fully reverse.

questions.stem: What should a patient do after each dose of an inhaled steroid?
questions.explanation: A is correct: rinse and spit after any inhaled steroid to prevent thrush, a yeast infection. B is not the counseling point taught for steroid side effects. C adds a drug that is not needed. D does not remove steroid from the mouth.

questions.stem: A man with an enlarged prostate starts tiotropium. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tiotropium is a long-acting muscarinic antagonist

questions.explanation: A, B, and C are correct: tiotropium is a muscarinic antagonist that can cause dry mouth and trouble urinating, especially with an enlarged prostate. D is wrong because tiotropium is a bronchodilator, not a steroid. E applies to inhaled steroids, which cause thrush.

questions.stem: A patient's asthma is not controlled on their current inhaler. What should be checked before stepping up therapy?
questions.explanation: A is correct: before stepping up, check inhaler technique, because poor technique looks just like drug failure. B, C, and D are not the checks that explain an inhaler not working.
